Variants.Content: Noble boys often served as page boys first, and later became squires of knights or lords. Attendants should take care of horses, clean armor, carry shields and spears, help their masters wear armor, and also learn riding, swordsmanship, heraldry, etiquette, and management. During the war, they followed their masters into camps and even battlefields, facing mud, wounds and fear before the glorious story happened. Clientel relationships can build cross-family trust and are a gentle form of hostage, educational, and political ties. Those who perform well may be knighted, but birth, wealth, and patronage still profoundly affect opportunities; serving a bad master may also teach a boy cruelty rather than honor.

A knight regards a good squire as a future comrade, or he may only regard him as a convenient servant. The real teaching does not come from lecturing, but from how the young man sees his master treating the weak every day.

Commoner children envy attendants' access to armor and war horses, but they may not see that this road requires family names and recommendations. Those of lower-class origin must prove their qualifications to stay earlier than the children of nobles.

The priest hopes that the squire will learn the virtues of chivalry, while the bachelor pays more attention to reading, writing and judgment. Both understand that a boy who only knows how to wield a sword can easily grow into a man who only knows how to create new enemies.

Lords and merchants viewed retainers as an enforceable order.
